rationale: The deficit penalty is sign-inconsistent when applied to a numerator that can be negative — inflating the denominator makes loss-making, deficit-laden firms' cash-flow yields *less* negative and therefore rank *higher*, exactly reversing the intended trap-avoidance mechanism that worked when the numerator was always-positive cash (che).

This is a cosmetic respecification of the archived Idle-Asset Value Trap (same at/mktcap × NEG(TREND(productivity)) template with sale/act swapped for gross-profit/at), and the productivity leg alone is close to a known declining-gross-profitability signal.

The min(oancf, ib+dp) construction is internally coherent and correctly implements the stated conservatism (it binds precisely when working-capital releases inflate cash flow), though it is structurally close to the archived Cash-Bounded Operating Claim Yield and the base leg is essentially the classic cash-flow-to-price anomaly.

A two-variable stock ratio with no genuine cross-theme interaction that essentially rediscovers the well-documented cash-holdings/net-cash-to-price anomaly, and it sits adjacent to the archived Enterprise Earned-Cash Discount family.

This mechanically bolts the deficit denominator from one archived signal onto the archived Liability-Productivity Sales Value expression, and the adjustment misfires in the same direction problem: when the EBITDA/liability trend is negative, shrinking the valuation leg for deficit firms makes the product *less* negative and thus ranks the worst firms higher.

The expression is internally consistent with the stated negative sign (cheap assets × large unexplained accrual magnitude), and the absolute-value opacity framing is a defensible departure from the weak signed reconciliation predecessor, though it overlaps conceptually with known accrual-quality/earnings-opacity effects and the multiplicative scaling makes the value leg mostly a magnitude amplifier.
